source: Wells et al. (2016) pre-engineering vs non-engineering high school students, FBS protocol study
finding: Null result. High school students with pre-engineering courses did not differ from those without on any FBS design issue or process. The hypothesis that they synthesise more was rejected.
numbers: 40 juniors in dyads, 45 min, window-opener task. Two coders per protocol; intercoder agreement 85-95%; 200-700 segments per session. Synthesis t=-1.01, p=0.163. Closest to significant: expected behaviour p=0.053, Reformulation II p=0.064, Analysis p=0.077. Structure about 40% of effort in both groups. Reformulation I about 30%.
limits: Small convenience sample, 3 rural schools, one task, no effect sizes, df and tails not stated, year 1 only. A null is not proof of equivalence.
agent_relevance: FBS code distributions are insensitive to a weak education difference. Do not expect an FBS-state scaffold to be validated by distribution shifts in small samples.

source: Wells et al. (2016) coding workload and reliability
finding: Human FBS coding needs two coders per transcript plus arbitration. This cost keeps studies small.
numbers: 6 coders, 40 protocols, 2 independent coders each; agreement 85-95%.
limits: Percent agreement, not kappa.
agent_relevance: FBS labels are a human-agreed construct. An LLM labeller should be checked against two-coder arbitrated data, not one rater.

source: Wells et al. (2016) near-significant trends
finding: Pre-engineering students leaned toward less expected behaviour and Reformulation II and more Analysis, but none crossed p<0.05.
numbers: Be t=-1.7 p=0.053; Reformulation II t=-1.59 p=0.064; Analysis t=1.48 p=0.077; Formulation t=1.22 p=0.118; Evaluation p=0.436.
limits: About 16 uncorrected tests; tails unknown. Signal is weak.
agent_relevance: Do not build rules on weak trends.

source: Williams, Paretti, Lee, Gero (2012) design education and sophomore design cognition, FBS coding
finding: Mechanical engineering sophomores (design course) vs engineering mechanics (control) showed differences in FBS issues and processes, but no significance test was possible.
numbers: 20 participants in semester 1 (17 ME, 3 EM), 16 in semester 2 (13 ME, 3 EM). Issues: structure 33-41%, behaviour from structure 24-32%, description 10-18%, expected behaviour 6-14%, function 2-7%, requirement 3-5%. Processes: Reformulation I 30-33%, Analysis 23-30%, Documentation 11-20%, Evaluation 8-17%, Synthesis 6-9%, Reformulation II 3-7%, Reformulation III 1-4%, Formulation about 2%.
limits: Control group only 3 per semester so significance could not be tested. Typical reliability 85-95% by Delphi arbitration.
agent_relevance: Real designers spend very little effort on function and formulation (2-7% and about 2%) and mostly on structure and analysis. A scaffold that forces function-first would depart from observed practice.

source: Williams et al. (2012) causal limit
finding: Authors say the data support correlation, not causation, between design-based education and design cognition. Experimental confirmation is still needed.
numbers: 3-year longitudinal plan; only year 1 reported; 3 EM controls per semester.
limits: Observational, not randomised; curricula differ in more than design content.
agent_relevance: Effects of design training on FBS profiles are not causally shown.

source: Song, Becker, Gero, DeBerard, Lawanto, Reeve (2016) problem decomposition and recomposition: freshmen, seniors, engineers
finding: Professional engineer dyads decompose and recompose problems more than students. Freshman and senior dyads did not differ. Students use depth-first decomposition, experts breadth-first.
numbers: 50 participants in dyads: 20 freshmen, 20 seniors, 10 experts (tests on 10, 10 and 5 dyads). Decomposition mean: freshmen 15.13% (SD 2.66), seniors 15.22% (3.27), engineers 22.38% (3.01). Recomposition: 15.28, 15.31, 22.57. Freshmen vs engineers p<.001, d=2.55; seniors vs engineers p=.010, d=2.28; freshmen vs seniors p=.496. Level effort: engineers vs students d 0.83-1.40.
limits: Authors call it a pilot and say N is too small to generalise. 5 engineer dyads, so large d is unstable. Intercoder reliability held above 80%.
agent_relevance: Expert breadth-first decomposition across system, interaction and subsystem levels is a measured but small-sample difference. It supports a state that tracks level and prefers breadth first.

source: Song et al. (2016) interview findings on problem definition
finding: Engineers considered many more factors when defining the problem. Freshman dyads focused on the device only; most seniors focused on the device but did better; few mentioned the accessibility standard or cost.
numbers: Qualitative interviews after the session. Students spent less cognitive effort on problem definition.
limits: Self-report after the task; dyads counted informally.
agent_relevance: Expert advantage is partly in framing and requirement breadth before structure. This fits a problem-space-first step with a stakeholder and constraint checklist.

source: Luo, Becker, Gero, Villanueva Alarcon, Lawanto (2021) systems thinking in engineering design, expert vs novice
finding: On a larger sample from the same protocol family, professionals and seniors looked alike and first-year students differed. This does not match Song 2016, where seniors matched freshmen.
numbers: 61 teams of 2 (122 people): 18 professionals (10+ years), 19 seniors, 24 first-years; 1-hour window-opener task. Coder agreement 80%, Cohen kappa 0.78. Level means (L1, L2, L3): professionals .12,.34,.46; seniors .14,.30,.48; first-year .06,.23,.64; ANOVA p=.000 each for L1-L3; partial eta squared 0.336 for levels. Professionals vs seniors p=.679,.264,.845; professionals vs first-year p=.001,.006,.000. System-process effect sizes 0.22-0.25. Decomposition plus recomposition 17% for pros and seniors, 13% for first-years.
limits: Mostly white male, one university, one task, cohort comparison not longitudinal. Conflicts with Song 2016 on seniors.
agent_relevance: Conflict inside one lab network: the expertise effect is solid for first-years vs the rest, not for seniors. First-years stay at detail (64% at level 3). An agent should force a top-level pass before detail.

source: Luo et al. (2021) Markov model of level transitions
finding: Professionals and seniors spend about twice as much time at the whole-system level and 1.5 times more at the middle level than first-years.
numbers: Level 1: 0.12 and 0.14 vs 0.06; level 3: 0.46 and 0.48 vs 0.64. Markov effect sizes 0.17-0.36 (called large); correspondence analysis dimension 1 explains 95.6% of variance.
limits: Effect-size labels follow loose conventions; level coding is a researcher choice.
agent_relevance: Gives a target profile (about 12-14% whole-system, 30-34% middle, 46-48% detail) a level-tracking state could be tested against.

source: Luo et al. (2021) limitations
finding: Authors say sample was mostly white male from a single large US public university, with gender, race and discipline effects not examined.
numbers: 122 participants, 61 teams; kappa 0.78, agreement 80%; experts defined as 10+ years or 10,000 hours.
limits: No cross-cultural data.
agent_relevance: No evidence on culture or individual-difference moderators; do not claim universality.

source: Synthesis of Wells 2016, Song 2016, Luo 2021 on expertise and FBS profiles
finding: Same window-opening task and same lab network. Weak education differences (Wells) were null; expert vs student differences were large with hierarchy coding (Luo, Song). Seniors matched professionals in Luo and matched freshmen in Song.
numbers: Luo partial eta squared 0.336; Song d up to 2.55; Wells all p>0.05. Sample sizes 40, 50, 122.
limits: One task, one lab cluster; no independent replication found outside this network. Coding differs (FBS issues vs hierarchy levels).
agent_relevance: Hierarchy-level coding separates expertise better than raw FBS-issue proportions. Prefer level and transition features over F/B/S counts.

source: Gero and Milovanovic (2020) framework for studying design thinking through minds, bodies and brains (Design Science 6, e19)
finding: Review of how FBS is used as a coding scheme. States that over 10,000 hours of industrial systems design have been FBS-coded and the two FBS papers have over 3,500 citations.
numbers: FBS papers over 3,500 citations (Google Scholar, 15 Jan 2020). Bott and Mesmer: over 10,000 hours coded. Domains: architecture, engineering, software, systems design. Each protocol coded several times by at least two coders.
limits: Written by the framework's originator; counts usage, not independent validity tests. Authors say studies are small because of coding cost.
agent_relevance: Popularity is not validation. Most evidence comes from one network of labs and one coding scheme.

source: Gero and Milovanovic (2020) review: dual-process finding and second-order codes
finding: Reports that all student and professional designers across several FBS protocol studies show both fast (System 1) and slow (System 2) design thinking. Expertise changes decomposition and recomposition effort. New and surprising codes were added to track creativity over time.
numbers: Gero and Song (2017): effort in decomposing and recomposing differs by expertise. Gero, Yu and Wells (2019): augmented code used to study a capstone course effect on high school students' creative design.
limits: No numbers in the review; second-hand.
agent_relevance: Both fast and slow modes exist in every group. A scaffold should not assume experts only intuit or novices only analyse.

source: Gero and Milovanovic (2020) review: stated limits and automation direction
finding: Names limits: measures may miss the complexity of design thinking, lab studies lack realism, studies are small. Proposes automating protocol analysis with machine learning trained on already coded protocols.
numbers: 40-page review; no numbers.
limits: Pre-LLM (2020). Automation is a stated direction, not a result.
agent_relevance: Automated FBS coding is a known open need; early LLM labelling work answers it only partly.

source: Gero and Milovanovic (2020) co-design and architectural critique distributions
finding: Reports FBS process distributions from 10 co-design protocols and 9 architectural critiques, and meta-codes (problem space R, F, Be; solution space S, Bs) to track co-evolution.
numbers: 10 co-design protocols, 9 critiques (Milovanovic and Gero 2020); numbers only in figures.
limits: Figures not machine-readable; second-hand.
agent_relevance: Problem/solution meta-coding is a cheap state feature for co-evolution tracking.

source: Kannengiesser and Gero (2019) Design thinking, fast and slow: a framework for Kahneman's dual-system theory in design (Design Science 5, e10)
finding: Adds a ninth FBS process, F to S (called 2 prime), as the fast System 1 route: a catalogue lookup without verification. Maps four design instances (fixation, case-based design, pattern-language design, brainstorming) onto fast or slow thinking.
numbers: 8 original processes plus 1 new; 4 design instances; cites over 3,000 citations for the FBS papers and 10,000+ hours of FBS coding.
limits: Theoretical; reports no data of its own. Authors say validation by protocol re-analysis is still needed; the added step bends the original no-function-in-structure rule.
agent_relevance: A fast function-to-structure lookup with no check is the failure mode that G1 and G3 guard against. The scaffold can allow a fast path but must never count it as verified.

source: Kannengiesser and Gero (2019) hypotheses H1 and H2 (search snippet only)
finding: Conference version tests H1 (design thinking has both systems) and H2 (professionals use system 1 more than students) on engineer and student protocols. Snippet says it supports existence of both.
numbers: H2 result not seen; no numbers retrieved.
limits: Only a search snippet seen; host refused connection. Do not use the H2 outcome.
agent_relevance: Do not cite the H2 outcome until read.

source: Wikipedia: Function-Behaviour-Structure ontology
finding: Lists the model: 3 categories, 8 processes (formulation, synthesis, analysis, evaluation, documentation, reformulation I, II, III), situated version with 3 worlds, 12 categories and 20 processes. Notes the ontology was critiqued for completeness (Galle 2009; Dorst and Vermaas 2005; Vermaas and Dorst 2007; Ralph 2010).
numbers: 3 categories; 8 processes; situated FBS 3 worlds, 4 interaction classes, 12 categories, 20 processes; extended FCBPSS has 6 categories.
limits: Secondary source; critique arguments not summarised.
agent_relevance: Rival ontologies and the completeness critique mean FBS is one lens, not settled.

source: AI- and ontology-based enhancements to FMEA for advanced systems engineering (arXiv 2511.17743, 2025)
finding: Review uses FBS as the function-modelling base for AI failure analysis. Its Table 2 shows authors define behaviour in at least 8 different ways (Gero 1990, Umeda 1995, Vermaas and Dorst 2007, Galle 2009 and others).
numbers: Quoted results from other work: 96% failure-classification accuracy, classifier 88.8%, fault classification 98.18%, text-mining precision and recall 86.6-93.2%, DeBERTa-v3 88.5% balanced accuracy, F1 0.89 with under 10% of labels.
limits: Narrative review; numbers are other studies' results, not FBS-specific tests. Notes LLM hallucination and suggests ontologies or knowledge graphs for grounding.
agent_relevance: With no agreed meaning of behaviour, an LLM given FBS labels may drift. Pair labels with definitions and examples.

source: arXiv 2511.17743: model-based systems engineering barriers and FBS role
finding: Reports industrial barriers: resistance, inconsistent standards, high model cost, unclear return on investment. Says FBS with ontologies aids traceability and reduces conceptual errors.
numbers: No new data; cites Cameron and Adsit (2020), Eisenbart and Gericke (2020).
limits: The conceptual-error claim is not tested by a controlled comparison.
agent_relevance: Treat the claim that FBS reduces conceptual errors as unproven.

source: Sahadevan et al. (2024) automated FBS knowledge graphs from product catalogues (arXiv 2412.05868): human and ChatGPT labelling
finding: Humans disagree on FBS labels. Three FBS experts applying the rules scored 54%, 93% and 87%. ChatGPT following the rules scored about 78%, then 100% after the rules were refined on the same items.
numbers: Experts 54%, 93%, 87%. ChatGPT 78% then 100% (rules tuned on the same items, so not held out).
limits: One partner company, electrical configurator components. The 100% is tuned-on-sample.
agent_relevance: FBS labelling is rule-sensitive. Labels need held-out checks (G3), not tuned-on-the-sample accuracy.

source: Sahadevan et al. (2024) final classifier test
finding: The final rule-based classifier did best on function and worst on behaviour.
numbers: 31 test items. Accuracy 71%. Function precision 73, recall 100, F1 85 (n=11). Behaviour 57/57/57 (n=7). Structure 78/54/64 (n=13). Macro F1 68, weighted F1 70.
limits: Tiny class counts; one company; authors say rules need adjusting for other domains.
agent_relevance: If behaviour labels are noisy, do not gate transitions on them alone.

source: Sahadevan et al. (2024) boundary case: geometry
finding: Rules required moving an artefact's geometry from structure to behaviour, because geometry assumes rigidity, which is a behaviour.
numbers: Rules refined over biweekly meetings and 3 expert reviews.
limits: Case study; product catalogues lack context.
agent_relevance: The B versus S boundary is a judgement call; define by example in any prompt.

source: Elhambakhsh, Grandi, Ko (2025) adapting LLMs for conceptual design: function classification of mechanical assembly parts (arXiv 2505.01627)
finding: Fine-tuning GPT-3.5 Turbo on 681 function-labelled parts raised test accuracy from about 4% to about 90%. Off-the-shelf GPT models did poorly at this function classification.
numbers: OSDR 15,636 samples, 7,568 unique parts; matched ABC set 6,786 unique parts. Fine-tuned test accuracy: 10% data (681) 0.89, 30% 0.84, 50% 0.75, 75% 0.68, 90% 0.63. Pre-trained GPT-3.5 Turbo 0.04, GPT-4 Turbo 0.27, GPT-4o mini 0.20. About 99% of generated labels fell in predefined classes.
limits: More training data lowered test accuracy, which the authors tie to class imbalance, so it is a warning not a scaling law. Single run, no confidence intervals, one dataset, fixed function taxonomy.
agent_relevance: Plain prompting of general models did badly on function labelling (4-27%). Domain-specific fine-tuning helped. Check on held-out data.

source: Elhambakhsh et al. (2025) augmentation step
finding: Uses the fine-tuned LLM to label ABC parts and then generates assembly samples guided by the function distribution.
numbers: Metrics: accuracy, precision, recall, F1 (weighted, macro, micro).
limits: Does not test design quality with people.
agent_relevance: Function classification is not design; do not read it as evidence of better design.

source: Chen, Zuo, Cai, Yin, Zhang, Sun, Childs, Wang (2024) Toward controllable generative design: FBS ontology with LLMs (J Mech Des 146(12))
finding: Splits a design task into functional, behavioural and structural reasoning steps with prompt templates and specification signifiers. In a comparative experiment, the approach scored highest; concepts were rated more novel, useful, functional and low-cost than the baseline.
numbers: Abstract has no statistics. Journal vol 146 issue 12, accepted 2024-05-14.
limits: Only the abstract page was opened; the PDF refused download, so sample size, raters, baseline and tests are unknown. Author-built method tested by its authors.
agent_relevance: The only direct LLM plus FBS prompting test found. Sign of benefit, size unknown; needs reproduction.

source: Joshi et al. (2025) Leveraging large language models for design by analogy: a computational framework (ICED25)
finding: Five-phase pipeline (retrieval, mapping, transfer, evaluation, storage) uses FBS as a cross-domain representation and LLMs for extraction, embeddings and analogy. One qualitative case, motorcycle design.
numbers: No quantitative results; one case; similarity threshold not given; no model named.
limits: Authors say FBS as cross-domain translator needs rigorous testing; scalability and LLM reliability and memorisation unevaluated.
agent_relevance: FBS as a schema for analogy transfer is proposed, not shown. Link to analogy subfield.
